content: Obstetrics and gynecology, commonly abbreviated as OB/GYN or O&G, are two surgical specialties that focus on the female reproductive system. These specialties are often combined into a single medical field and postgraduate training program. This integrated training equips OB/GYN practitioners to manage the full range of clinical and surgical conditions affecting the female reproductive organs and to provide care for both pregnant and non-pregnant patients. The training required to become an OB/GYN is rigorous. For instance, in Australia, the residency training period lasts six years, which is among the longest for any specialty, rivaled only by neurosurgery. In the United States, the pathway involves four years of undergraduate education at an accredited college or university, followed by four years of medical school and an additional four years of residency training. After completing residency, some OB/GYN surgeons choose to pursue further subspecialty training through fellowship programs, which can last one to four years and often include a research component alongside clinical and surgical training. However, the majority of OB/GYNs enter private or academic practice as generalists. Examples of subspecialty training available in the United States include: Maternal-Fetal Medicine: This obstetrical subspecialty focuses on the medical and surgical management of high-risk pregnancies. Reproductive Endocrinology and Infertility: This gynecologic subspecialty addresses the medical and surgical evaluation of women with menstrual cycle disorders and fertility issues. Gynecologic Oncology: This subspecialty is dedicated to the medical and surgical treatment of cancers affecting the female reproductive organs. Urogynecology and Pelvic Reconstructive Surgery: This field focuses on diagnosing and surgically treating conditions such as urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse. It is sometimes incorrectly referred to by laypersons as female urology. Other areas of focus, such as advanced laparoscopic surgery, family planning (including contraception and sometimes pregnancy termination), pediatric and adolescent gynecology, and menopausal and geriatric gynecology, are considered informal concentrations rather than formally recognized subspecialties. Of these, only the first four subspecialties are officially recognized by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) and the American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ABOG). To achieve board certification in a subspecialty, a practitioner must complete an ACGME-accredited fellowship and pass an additional standardized examination to obtain a Certificate of Added Qualifications (CAQ). In rural areas of the United States, particularly west of the Mississippi River, it is not uncommon for general practitioners to provide obstetrical services. However, these generalists typically lack training in the surgical aspects of obstetrics and gynecology and should not be confused with residency-trained, board-certified OB/GYNs. All gynecologists are trained obstetricians, but the reverse is not necessarily true. Some OB/GYNs may choose to discontinue the obstetric component of their practice and focus exclusively on gynecology, especially as they age. This decision is often influenced by the demanding hours associated with obstetrics and, in some countries, the high risk of litigation. In recent years, medical malpractice lawsuits and rising insurance premiums have led many American obstetricians and gynecologists to reduce or abandon their practices. Between 2000 and 2003, fewer medical students chose to specialize in obstetrics, resulting in a critical shortage of obstetricians in some states and fewer healthcare options for women. However, this shortage also led to higher average salaries for OB/GYNs, as noted in an article by Medical Economics. Starting in 2004, state legislation mandating tort reform, combined with the ACGME's decision to limit resident work hours, contributed to a gradual resurgence in the number of medical students selecting OB/GYN as a specialty. By the 2007 medical residency match, only six OB/GYN training spots remained vacant across the entire United States—a record low that highlighted the specialty's growing competitiveness, comparable to other surgical fields.
